blocks.heading: Regional and global energy links
blocks.text: For many years Namibia generated less than half of the electricity it used; in December 2025 local generation accounted for 51.6% of electricity supplied to the domestic economy. The rest is imported through the Southern African Power Pool. It has long relied mainly on South Africa, and also has purchase agreements with Botswana, Zambia, Zimbabwe, the DRC and Mozambique. The 950 km Caprivi Link, opened in 2010 between Gerus in central Namibia and Katima Mulilo, connects Namibia to the northern part of the power pool. Imports depend on spare supply in partner countries and on line capacity.

blocks.text: Regional supply can also transmit disruption. Reduced generation or constrained transmission elsewhere can affect import options, while shared planning and diverse connections can reduce some risks. Domestic generation, regional trade, maintenance and demand management therefore interact. A balanced explanation recognises both the opportunity of cooperation and the practical limits of relying on a particular route or source.

Namibia has no oil refinery, so all its petrol, diesel and other refined fuels are imported, mainly by ship through Walvis Bay. When world oil prices rise or the Namibia dollar weakens, the import bill and pump prices rise. Transport, mining, farming and diesel generators then cost more to run.

Energy security is consequently a supply-chain question. A local generator may still need imported fuel or components, while a renewable installation may reduce fuel imports but require maintenance equipment. Regional and global links are part of the system rather than evidence that local resources have no value. Assess the diversity, reliability, affordability and environmental effects of the actual connections supporting the required service.
